findings: The api never reads `permissions.ask`. Claude Code's docs say an ask rule makes one of the read-only commands ask, and in dontAsk anything that asks is denied. So a repository whose `.claude/settings.json` has `ask: ["Bash(cat:*)"]` gets a Capabilities page that shows `cat` solid under "Claude Code's read-only commands do not ask" on a dontAsk step, and that step's `cat` is denied. This is the reverse of the claim item 30 set out to remove. The gap is written down only in commit 0fba515's body, in no doc a person reads (not features.md, not the plan). Either handle `ask` rules the way deny rules are handled for those commands, or record the gap where the page's other open items live.

This test checks the dated `READ_ONLY_COMMANDS.measured` list against the repository's current `.claude/settings.json`. Suppose someone later adds `Bash(ls:*)` or `Bash(cat:*)` to `permissions.allow`, which is a harmless change. `npm test` then fails, and the failure says the 2026-09-15 measurement is wrong and should be demoted. It isn't wrong: it was taken under the settings of that day. The guard is only meaningful when someone edits the data, and it will break for an unrelated settings change. Pin the allow list the measurement ran under inside the test or the data, rather than reading the live file.

Two small findings on the path where a queued card's start fails without a refusal: git's error is printed on every pass, and a daemon started after the failure never mentions the card. Both are worth a person's attention but not another round.
findings: The `git` helper calls `execFileSync` without `stdio`, so Node copies git's stderr to the process's own stderr as well as putting it in the error message. Before this change only a person's `wf start` reached it, once. Now `startQueued` (runner.ts:1244, via `startFromInbox` → `start` → `makeWorkspace`) retries a card that failed without a refusal on every pass. A queued card whose `repo:` is a folder with no git prints `fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git` on `wf up`'s terminal every 4 seconds, with no card name, for as long as it holds the queue. That contradicts the README's claim that `wf up` says it once. Running `node --test --test-name-pattern="fails without a refusal" test/queue-store.test.ts` shows four such lines for four passes. The test (queue-store.test.ts:563-577) only captures `console.log`, so it passes. Passing `stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']` to the helper keeps git's words in the error without the echo; a test that captures `process.stderr.write` over those passes would pin it.

`wf up` skips a queue line marked `again`, and `again` is judged against the try saved in `$WF_ROOT/queue/<name>.json` (runner.ts:1251), not against what this `wf up` process has printed. So a `wf up` started, or restarted, after the failure was written never names the card holding the queue: its first pass already reads `again: true`. queue-store.test.ts:574 pins exactly that, since its two `wf up` passes print nothing about `no-git-a1b2`, not even once. A person restarting the daemon to see why cards stopped starting gets no line about it; only `wf inbox` shows it. Remembering the last printed line in the `up` loop is presentation, not a decision the tick carries between passes, so it would not break the level-triggered rule.

I found two edge cases in how `writeWorkflow` removes files. Neither is reachable on the Linux (ext4) setup this runs on today, so neither is worth another round.
findings: Stale files are removed only after every step's file is written, and a name counts as stale unless it matches exactly. On a case-insensitive filesystem (macOS, or a repo on /mnt/c under WSL), renaming step `Review` to `review` goes wrong. `put('review.md')` reads or writes the existing `Review.md` entry. Then `Review.md` is not in `names`, so `rmSync` deletes that one file. The step's body is lost, the other steps' `after: review` now name no step, so the folder no longer loads, and the returned `steps` say it does. Removing stale files before writing, or comparing names case-folded, would fix it.

`e.isFile()` on a readdir Dirent is false for a symlink, but `loadWorkflows` reads a symlinked `old.md` as a step. If a folder has a symlinked step file that the save drops, the file is never removed. The folder then still reads that step, even though `steps` in the result leave it out. If that step waits on a step the save removed, the folder no longer loads, though the write reported success. And for a symlinked step file the save keeps, `fs.writeFileSync` (line 1052) writes through the link into whatever file it points at. Nobody links step files today (the api only documents linked folders), so this is low priority. It is still a gap in the promise that the folder reads back as the steps returned.

findings: The loop that writes the pasted schemas runs before the `try`, so only a `writeWorkflow` failure puts schemas back. A failure while writing a schema does not. Example: `a.schema.json` is new and `b.schema.json` is read-only on disk. `a.schema.json` gets written, writing `b.schema.json` throws EACCES, and the route returns 500 with `a.schema.json` left in the folder. No step names it, and the folder's version has changed. features.md (§ The board half, 'or the disk fail, each schema is put back as it was') promises otherwise. The 500 test only covers a failure inside `writeWorkflow`.

The banner says 'Not saved, and nothing written' for every error, including a 500 and a failed fetch. Neither guarantees that. `writeWorkflow` writes the step files one at a time, so on a disk failure partway (for example `[build, plan]` with `plan.md` a folder, EISDIR) `build.md` is already written. The api puts back only the schemas, and the board still says nothing was written. The same goes for a fetch cut off after the api wrote. Only a 4xx is known to have written nothing, so a 500 or a network error should say the folder may have been written and suggest reading it again.

Reviewed the whole change against §8 and ran the suite: `npm run typecheck` clean and `npx turbo run test --force` green at the claimed counts (agent-workflows 575/574+1 skipped, api 200, web 243, engine 326). The four asked-for items are there and genuinely tested — `workspace: main` with its refusals at parse and at load, the ending's gate held before the step is filed, `to decide` in both kinds, `wf decide`'s facts, and `ship.md` on the four dev folders with a real-git store test. Seven findings, none of which breaks the happy path: the two worth acting on before this is used in anger are that nothing stops two runs' ending steps working in the person's checkout at once, and that the ending step's brief still carries the artifacts contract telling it to leave files in that checkout for a run that collects and commits nothing there. The rest are refusal and screen messages that are wrong or unhelpful at the new gate.
findings: Nothing keeps two runs' ending steps out of the same checkout. `validate` refuses a second ending inside one workflow, but `workspaceFor` hands `run.repo` to any approved ending, and `tick` advances every run in one pass: approve two finished `dev` runs (the board's `to decide` list invites exactly that) and the next pass files both `ship` tasks with `cwd` = the repository, and the engine runs both at once (pool cap 2 by default). Both sessions read `git status --porcelain` as clean, both run `git merge --no-ff --no-commit`, and the loser's `git merge --abort` (step 5 of its own prose) throws away the winner's staged trial merge while the winner's `npm test` is running against it — two opus sessions wasted and the person's checkout rewritten under them. The only thing standing in the way is ship.md's prose, and the house rule is that the machinery refuses the alternative. A level-triggered refusal to file an ending while another run has one unsettled in the same repo (the store's other runs are already read for `forgetRefusal`) is the shape; there is no test for two runs at all.

The ending step gets the standard artifacts contract, whose second bullet is false for it and invites damage: "Or leave it in this workspace, and name it in `artifacts` by its path from the workspace root … the run copies each such file into that directory … A file left in the workspace is committed with the rest too." For a `workspace: main` step "this workspace" is the person's checkout, and `handOffDue` (run.ts:1132) now excludes the step, so `collectArtifacts` (runner.ts:1546) never runs and nothing is committed. A ship session that writes `merge-log.md` beside its closeout, as its brief tells it to, leaves an untracked file in the person's checkout for ever — and the next run's ship step then reads `git status --porcelain` as non-empty and signs off blocked at step 1 of its prose. It also contradicts ship.md's own "leave the checkout as you found it". Give a main-workspace step a contract with only the absolute-path bullet.

The send-back refusal at an ending's gate names the wrong step's gate and a command that is itself refused. On the shipped `dev` folders, `wf retry <run> review` (no --message) at ship's gate reaches the `sendsBack` branch added at run.ts:1317 and prints "review is awaiting approval: a try of it sends it back from its gate … — or approve it: wf approve <run> review." review is not awaiting approval (`wf ls` shows it `unverified · done`, ship `awaiting approval`), and `wf approve <run> review` is refused by `approvalRefusal` with "review has no gate … <run> is gated at ship." It should say ship is the step at its gate and name `wf approve <run> ship`. The test at test/run.test.ts:3320 does not catch it: `/^review is awaiting approval|--message/` is an alternation, so it passes whatever the sentence says.

`decision` does not apply `unheld`, so `wf decide` and the board contradict `wf ls` in the window the round-3 fix was meant to close. Between `wf retry <run> review --message "…"` and the pass that files it, `standing` still reads ship as `awaiting approval`: `wf decide` prints "AWAITING APPROVAL, waiting on you: ship — your approval is what runs it" and `gateLines` prints `wf approve <run> ship`, while `wf ls` (which does apply `unheld`) shows ship `waiting` with nothing to decide, and `wf approve <run> ship` is refused with "try 2 of review is asked for … approving now would take the result that ask objects to." The api's run page reads `decision` and `gateLines` too, so its Approve button is live in the same window. `decision` should take the same `unheld` adjustment `assess` and `listing` take.

`wf retry <run> ship` at the ending's gate — the step `wf ls` names on the line above the send-back — falls through to the default "ship is awaiting approval, and there is nothing to try again." Before this change every `awaiting approval` step had modes (a step with no followers hit the first `sendsBack` clause), so this state is new and lands on a message that names no fix: it should point at `wf approve <run> ship` and `wf retry <run> <the work> --message`, as `sendBackTo` already computes.

`wf round <run> review` at an ending's gate is refused with "…its loop is over and there is nothing to go round again. What waits on it has been filed: wf ls <run>." Nothing has been filed — ship is unfiled and waiting for the person's approval, which is the whole state they are standing in. `roundAsk`'s gate check at run.ts:1903 only looks inside `loopSpan`, so the ending's gate is invisible to it; the sentence should say the run is at its ending's gate and name `wf approve` / the send-back.

The board now tells a person to merge by hand a branch whose run has an ending step waiting to merge it. `commandsOf` offers `ship it  git merge --no-ff <branch>` and `drop it  git branch -D …` for any awaiting decision with branches, and a `dev` run parked at ship's gate is one — while `wf decide` deliberately suppresses both for a folder that merges (cli.ts:889, `!merges(steps)`). Outside your package, so the fix is one line for the board run (pass `merges(steps)` the way the CLI does); at minimum it belongs in features.md's "What it leaves", which does not name it.

summary: Reviewed the whole diff against the brief: the `supervisor` folder and its README, `slot: none` through the parser, `validate` and all three cap readers, the `taskPhases` earlier-tries gate, the `branchesToRead` base drop, the artifacts contract split, and the new tests. Ran `npx turbo run test --force` (agent-workflows 587 / 586 pass 1 skip, api 202, web and engine unchanged) and `npm run typecheck` — all green. I traced every consumer of `views` inside `advance` and every path to `spendOf` to satisfy myself the earlier-tries gate loses nothing, and confirmed the CLI's `wf decide` never reaches the fallback with a base branch for a run that cut worktrees. Three findings, none a machinery bug: a present-tense claim in the new brief that goes stale, the git prohibition left to prose where `disallow:` is available, and a board state the Shipped section undersells.
findings: The new brief for a `workspace: main` step whose run has no result branch ends with "The checkout is at `<run.baseRef>`" — a present-tense claim about the checkout, made from the sha frozen at `wf start`. `baseRef` is only ever rewritten for a run with `--after`, and the supervisor's run never ends in the one checkout every other run's `ship.md` merges into. From the first merge onwards every recomposed brief (one per answer, dozens over a day) names a commit several merges behind, and a session that acts on it — `git diff <baseRef>`, `git log <baseRef>..HEAD` — reads other runs' merges as the state it is responsible for: the same mistake round 3 removed from `wf decide`. The other sentence in the block, `results` "cut from `<baseRef>`", is a historical fact and stays true; only this one goes false. Nothing tests it: run.test.ts:295 asserts the sentence is present, not that what it says is still so on try 30. Say the base branch by name, or read HEAD where the brief is composed, or drop the clause.

"**Never type git for a run.** Not `git merge`, not `git branch -D`, not a push, not a checkout of its branch" is the most consequential rule in the brief and is enforced by nothing — against CLAUDE.md's *Prose is not a constraint*, and with no test that makes it refuse. The step works in the person's real checkout with the base branch checked out and has every tool but the four on line 14, so a `git merge <run branch>` lands work on main that no ending step trial-merged and no person approved; a `git checkout <run branch>` leaves the checkout off the base and stops the next `ship.md` at its step 1. `.claude/settings.json` already denies `Bash(git push:*)` and `Bash(git branch -D:*)`, so those two are real; it cannot deny `git merge` because `ship.md` runs in the same checkout and needs it — which makes this step's own `disallow:` (line 14) the only place the refusal can live. Either add the denies with a test that makes one refuse, or say in the folder's README why prose is the best available guard here.

"What it leaves" says of the board only that "a run that never ends is drawn as any other ... nothing says 'this one is the supervisor'". It is worse than that on the operator's first day: a step that signed off `blocked` is in `stopsFollowers`, so `assess` gives the run `failed`, and `RunStatus` on the board is `'running' | 'succeeded' | 'failed' | 'cancelled'` — the supervisor's normal, healthy, waiting-for-you state draws its card as a failed run for as long as it waits. `wf ls` is unaffected (its run line carries no status word), so the gap is the board's alone. One sentence in this bullet would keep the operator from reading the first question it asks as a crash.

findings: The link refusal tells the person to "copy what it points at over it, cp --remove-destination", which is GNU coreutils only. On macOS — the filesystem family the same function's case-insensitivity fix is written for — `cp` has no long options at all, so following the message gives `cp: illegal option -- -` and the person is left with a refusal whose named fix does not run. Either drop the flag from the sentence or name a portable pair (`rm <file> && cp <target> <file>`). The same sentence is duplicated in test/write-workflow.test.ts:263, so a fix touches both.
